A consumer app has grown to millions of active free users but converts under 2% to its paid tier, and investor patience with the losses is ending. Past monetization tests backfired: aggressive paywalls spiked uninstalls, and intrusive ads damaged app-store ratings within weeks. Usage data shows several distinct user segments that get very different value from the product.

Design a monetization strategy that meaningfully increases revenue per user while protecting retention and ratings. Choose and justify the mix of subscription tiers, usage-based pricing, advertising, and partnerships; map offers to the identified user segments; and define the experiment plan and guardrail metrics that will catch churn damage before it compounds.

agentResponses.content:
[PREVIOUS FRAMING, APPLIED SIDEWAYS]

Let me come at this from the side again, because the framing in the brief is doing quiet damage.

"Converts under 2%" invites a project called *conversion*. But 2% at millions of actives is roughly market-median for a consumer app, which means the number is not the anomaly — the anomaly is that almost none of the other 98% is monetised at all, in any form, and that a business has been built on the assumption that revenue arrives only through one door, at one price, from people who say yes to one question.

And note what the two failed tests had in common. A paywall that spiked uninstalls and ads that broke the ratings are the same manoeuvre twice: a broadcast tax, applied uniformly, perfectly visible to exactly the people best equipped to punish it. Nobody uninstalls over something they were *offered*. They uninstall over something that was *taken*. The whole of what follows is one idea in several costumes — convert taxes into choices, and let different people choose differently.

The objective, then, is not a higher conversion rate. It's net revenue per thousand monthly actives, held net of retention cost, arrived at by routes most of which are not called "paywall." And a rating, incidentally, is not a marketing metric. It's distribution. It behaves exactly like shelf space: slow to rebuild, fast to lose, and it silently sets the price of every install you buy thereafter. I'd treat any experiment that touches it as structurally different from one that doesn't — a point I'll come back to, because it dictates the entire test design.

**The decomposition I'd want before shipping anything**

Three weeks. Not a discovery phase. Three questions.

*Who actually got hurt last time, and were they ever going to pay?* The uninstall spike is almost certainly not uniform. My expectation — and it should be checked, because the whole plan turns on it — is that the loss was concentrated in recent, low-intent installs who had not yet reached a value moment, and that the tenured core absorbed the paywall with irritation rather than departure. If that's true, the lesson from the failed test is not "don't ask," it's "you asked before you'd earned the right to, of people who had no idea what they were declining." Those are opposite lessons and the business has probably drawn the wrong one.

Similarly on ads: I'd want the review text mined by topic and by *placement*, not the star average. Ratings damage from advertising is nearly always concentrated in a few specific sins — an interstitial on cold start, an ad interrupting a task already in flight, an unskippable unit in the core loop, an ad served in the first session. Ads in a surface that was already list-shaped and browse-shaped tend to pass almost unremarked. "Ads damaged ratings" is not a finding. It's an average concealing a design error.

*What does each segment cost to serve, and what does each contribute that isn't money?* This is the one most consumer businesses never do. Some free users consume real marginal cost — storage, inference, bandwidth, transcoding, support. Others cost approximately nothing and produce the content, the liquidity, or the social graph that makes the product worth using. Those two groups must never be treated with the same instrument. The first is a metering problem. The second is an asset you are currently mistaking for a cost, and the correct monetisation of an asset is to build something around it, not to charge it rent.

*What is the free tier actually for?* Right now it is almost certainly doing two jobs badly: it's the demo *and* it's the product. A demo should create a felt gap. A habit product should create dependence. A free tier assembled by subtraction — the product minus a few features nobody chose deliberately — does neither. Under 2% usually means there is no *reason* to pay that a user could articulate, and no amount of paywall optimisation fixes an absent reason.

Two numbers on one page, by segment: probability of ever paying, and cost to serve. The strategy lives in the four quadrants, and it's a different strategy in each.

**Segments, and what each one is for**

I'll use the shape these portfolios usually take; the names matter less than the principle that each gets a different instrument and that no instrument is applied to everybody.

*The habitual narrow users.* High frequency, shallow feature use, genuine dependence, low willingness to pay a professional price. Enormous in number. The mistake is offering them the full tier — they decline, and you record a "no" that was really a "not at that price." These want a cheap tier that removes their one specific friction, priced low enough to be a non-decision, sold annually. This is the single largest untapped pool and it requires a price point the business probably considers insultingly low.

*The depth users.* Broad feature use, high resource consumption, and the ones whose workflow would genuinely break without the product. They are already paying, or would. These want *more*, not cheaper: a higher tier with capability they'd otherwise assemble themselves, plus metered headroom above generous limits. The existing paid tier is probably underpriced for these people and overpriced for everyone else, which is what happens when one price carries a whole portfolio.

*The contributors.* Whoever creates what the others consume. Never charge them, and never degrade their experience for ad revenue. Monetise *around* them: give them free premium and take a share of what they earn, if there's anything to earn. A take rate is the most elegant instrument available in consumer software, because the payer's revenue arrives before yours and nobody experiences it as a price.

*The spiky ones.* They arrive with a task, complete it, and leave for four months. No subscription will ever fit them and every subscription pitch you show them is a small deposit of resentment. They want a day pass, a week pass, a credit pack, a one-time unlock. This cohort is usually written off as unmonetisable and is often worth more per person than the habitual users, because their intent at the moment of arrival is very high.

*The drive-bys.* Install, poke, gone within a week regardless of what you do. They cost nothing to lose and they are, simultaneously, the source of most one-star reviews — which means the correct treatment is *gentler* than instinct suggests, not harsher. Never monetise before first value. The ad load and the offers should escalate with tenure, not with desperation.

*The dormant.* Sizeable, cheap to reach, and best served by seasonal passes and win-back offers rather than by trying to restore a daily habit that was never there.

**The central move: give it away in order to sell it**

If I could ship one thing, it would be a reverse trial. Everyone new gets the full premium product for a fortnight without asking, without a card, and without a countdown clock shoved in their face. At the end, they land on a free tier that is genuinely good and deliberately designed — not crippled, but noticeably narrower than the two weeks they just had.

This inverts the psychology that broke the last attempt. A paywall takes something the user never had and is experienced as a wall. A reverse trial gives something and then narrows, and the resulting sensation is not resentment but *want*. It also does something the business badly needs and currently lacks: it produces high-quality intent data on every single new user, because their behaviour during the fortnight tells you which segment they're in far better than any survey. Conversion becomes a routing problem rather than a persuasion problem.

The guardrail: the post-trial free tier must be worth using on its own terms. If the fortnight ends and the product stops being useful, you've just built a slower paywall with a friendlier face, and the uninstall curve will find you eventually.

**The subscription ladder**

Three tiers, not one, and the spread should be wider than feels comfortable.

An entry tier at a price that looks like nothing — the price of a coffee, monthly — that solves one crisply nameable irritation for the habitual narrow segment. Its job is volume, and its job is *also* to be the thing that a hesitant user says yes to, because the second purchase from a paying user is dramatically easier than the first purchase from a free one. Treat it as a foot in the door rather than as revenue, and it becomes both.

A core tier roughly where the current single price sits, positioned as the default, presented in the middle where defaults get chosen.

A top tier priced considerably above what the business thinks the market will bear, aimed at the depth segment, bundling capability, headroom, early access, and — if the product has any professional application at all — the things people would otherwise expense. The reliable finding here is that a small tail of users will pay several times the current price and are currently paying once, because nobody has offered them anything else. That is money left on a table you own.

Annual plans pushed hard, with a discount that looks generous, because annual is not really a discount — it's a churn instrument, a cash instrument, and a way of removing eleven monthly opportunities to reconsider.

And regional pricing, properly done, on purchasing-power lines with local payment methods. This is dull, unglamorous, entirely uncontroversial, and in most consumer apps it is worth more than any clever packaging idea, largely because the millions of actives are almost never distributed the way the pricing is.

**Metering, which is pack architecture in a different costume**

Where the product consumes real marginal cost, meter it — but set the limits so high that only the top few percent ever notice, and communicate remaining allowance generously rather than ominously. The point of a limit is not to constrain the many; it's to create a legitimate, non-arbitrary reason for the few heavy users to pay in proportion to what they consume, which is the only pricing logic that both feels fair and scales with your costs.

Beside it, consumables for the spiky segment: credit packs, passes, one-time unlocks. These are a different transaction shape entirely, they capture people who will never sign a recurring commitment, and they have the pleasant property of arriving at the moment of highest intent.

**Advertising, redesigned rather than reduced**

The instinct after the last attempt will be to abandon ads. I'd resist it, because you tested one implementation and concluded something about the category.

What I'd ship instead, in order of increasing risk:

*Rewarded, opt-in units.* The user chooses to watch something in exchange for a credit, an unlock, a day of premium. This is the loyalty-mechanic idea from the grocery problem in another form: it reaches only the price-sensitive user who selects into it, leaves the experience of everyone else untouched, is invisible to your ratings because nobody reviews an app badly for something they chose, and — usefully — it monetises exactly the population that has already declined to pay. It converts a hard no into a small yes, repeatedly.

*Native placements in surfaces that are already browse-shaped.* Feeds, discovery, search results, recommendations. Ads here are read as content rather than interruption, provided the density is low and the labelling honest.

*Escalation by tenure and by inferred willingness to pay, never uniformly.* Zero ads before first value. Zero ads for contributors. Zero ads for anyone the model scores as likely to subscribe soon — you don't put a coin-operated turnstile in front of a customer who's reaching for their wallet. Meaningful load for tenured non-payers who've declined the ladder three times.

*Never*: interstitials on cold start, anything unskippable inside the core loop, anything that interrupts a task already begun, anything in the first session. Those four rules would, I suspect, have prevented most of the earlier damage on their own.

And an ad-load ceiling written down in advance — a number, owned by a named person, that revenue targets are not permitted to raise. I'll come back to why that matters more than it sounds.

**Partnerships, which are the channel argument again**

Most consumer apps treat partnerships as business development garnish. They're better understood as a way to sell the same asset into channels where the realised price is set by someone other than the app store and the comparison-shopping user.

*Bundled distribution.* Carriers, device makers, super-apps, subscription aggregators, broadband and insurance packages. The economics are worse per user and dramatically better in aggregate, because the payer isn't the user, the churn is contractual, and the acquisition cost is zero. This is the single most under-pursued route for an app with millions of actives and a weak direct conversion rate, because scale is the qualification.

*The side door into organisations.* Employers, schools, health plans, professional bodies — whoever benefits from the outcome your users get. Same product, a completely separate conversation, a completely separate price, and no exposure to app-store dynamics at all. If even a thin slice of your actives use the product in a context someone else would fund, that's a business rather than a feature.

*Commerce and affiliate, where intent is legible.* Only where the recommendation would have been made anyway; the moment the ranking bends toward the payer, you've traded the product for a quarter's revenue.

*A developer surface* for the depth segment — API, embeds, integrations — priced by usage. Small, and it converts your most demanding users from a support cost into a channel.

I'd hold the line that no channel gets to borrow another channel's price, and I'd expect the leak to come from inside: someone will want to run a lifetime deal, or match the bundled price direct, and within a year the ladder will be flat again.

**The experiment plan**

This is where I'd be most insistent, because the sequencing is the strategy.

*Order matters, and it's set by reversibility.* Pricing and packaging tests are reversible; ratings damage is not. So: instrumentation and segmentation first, then packaging and the reverse trial, then the ladder and regional pricing, then metering and consumables, then advertising last and most cautiously. Not because ads matter least, but because they're the only instrument that can damage the asset you can't rebuild.

*A permanent, unmonetised holdout.* Two to five percent of users, never shown a paywall, an ad, or an offer, forever. Expensive, argued about annually, and the only way you will ever know the true cumulative cost of monetisation on retention and lifetime value. Every individual test will look fine against a control that has itself been progressively degraded. The holdout is the only honest baseline, and the businesses that skip it discover the damage three years later as an unexplained decay in organic growth.

*Ring-fence the irreversible risk geographically.* Anything touching ad load or interruption gets tested first in markets whose store ratings don't feed global discovery and whose revenue contribution is small enough to lose. That gives you a real read on rating velocity and review sentiment before the instrument ever touches the markets that matter. This one design choice is worth more than any amount of statistical sophistication.
